newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - London stocks strong, dollar consolidates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - London stocks strong, dollar consolidates.

text.p: The London stock market moved within 10 points of its record high on Tuesday morning but other major European bourses put on a mixed performance and the dollar lost a little of the ground it had won recently against the yen.
Investors, meanwhile, bailed out of precious metals and gold hit its lowest level for 18 months.

In a currency market on the watch for problems with European monetary union, the mark rose to 1,001.70 lire after French President Jacques Chirac said Italy might not be among the first countries to join a single European currency in 1999.
But it soon slipped back to near its previous close of 998.
With interest rate concerns also very much on investors' minds, markets focused on September data for the U.S. National Association of Purchasing Managers (NAPM) index at 1400 GMT.
The figures, leading up to Friday's key U.S. September jobs data, will provide fresh clues on the next move in U.S. rates.
Higher futures prices prompted London shares to push nearer to record levels and the key 4,000 level on the FTSE 100 index.

"Most people expected a steady start and consolidation at the start to the new quarter but we've been proved to be wrong. The futures came in strongly and have been trading abover 4,000 for much of the morning," said one senior trader.
"We won't have difficulty breaking the 4,000 mark in the cash market, maybe not today, but in the next day or two."
The stock market shrugged off news of a higher-than-expected British September purchasing managers index -- 53.4 against a forecast 51.9 -- which could suggest higher interest rates.
But the Frankfurt bourse made only limited gains and Paris was slightly lower.

For European stock markets, Wall Street gave a limited lead overnight, with the Dow Jones industrial average of blue-chip shares ending up 9.25 points to 5,882.17 but short of a new all-time high after a late sell-off in technology stocks.
The dollar hit 2-1/2 year highs against the yen on Monday, boosted by signs that Japan's economic revival was faltering and the gap between U.S. and Japanese interest rates was widening.

It showed a limited decline from its highs on Tuesday on profit-taking after key Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara denied that he had said Japan was unlikely to raise rates until the end of March 1997.
"We have seen some profit-taking but most of it has been overnight," said one London bank dealer.

After comments by Finance Minister Wataru Kubo that he supported a strong dollar, not necessarily a stronger dollar, an official of his ministry said Kubo's comments did not mean Tokyo did not want the dollar to rise further against the yen.

"I think the Japanese authorities don't want to rock the boat. They want the dollar to stay around these levels," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. "It helps the profitability of Japanese companies and helps foster the economic recovery."
Gold traded around $377.35 an ounce by the end of the morning, down from Monday's London close of $378.60. Other precious metals slipped lower in its wake.

Bullion began to slide last week when mainly U.S.-owned investment funds switched to more attractive stock and bond markets. Investors had already been jolted by talks on plans to sell some International Monetary Fund gold reserves.
CURRENCIES AT 1115 GMT
The dollar was trading around 111.19 yen and 1.5255 marks, below Monday's late European levels of 111.52 and 1.5255.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1115 GMT
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares was up 27.1 points at 3,980.8 after an earlier high of 3,984.5. Its all-time peak was 3,994.1.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was down 4.26 at 2,128.55. The 30-share DAX index of German shares was up 4.60 at 2,656.45.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $377.05/ounce in the morning, its lowest fixing since March 1995 and below Monday's afternoon fix of $379.00 and close of $378.60. Silver eased two cents to $4.85.
